items.item: Key groups existing as a layer between individual keys and operator instances is what makes rescaling tractable at all — without it, every rescale would require recomputing a hash assignment for every single key rather than moving a small, fixed number of pre-sorted blocks.

at.step: Reveal: every key hashes into a fixed key group

items.item: Max parallelism being fixed at job-creation time, not adjustable without a full state migration, is the direct consequence of key groups being the unit of redistribution — the number of groups has to be decided before any key is ever assigned to one.

at.step: Reveal: rescaling moves whole key groups, never splitting one

items.item: RocksDB's slower per-access cost isn't a tuning problem to optimize away — it's the direct, necessary cost of state that physically lives on disk rather than in memory, the same trade this chapter's object-storage topics make for durability elsewhere.

at.step: Reveal: heap and RocksDB trade speed for capacity

items.item: Recovery time being driven purely by state size, not job complexity, means a capacity-planning exercise that budgets recovery time by counting operators is measuring the wrong variable entirely — the right question is how much state a single instance is allowed to accumulate.

at.step: Reveal: recovery time tracks state, not the job's shape

items.item: State TTL and schema evolution both look like generic flexibility features from their names alone, but each is scoped narrowly on purpose — TTL only promises best-effort, not guaranteed-instant cleanup, and schema evolution explicitly excludes key structure and Kryo-serialized types.

at.step: Reveal: TTL expires idle state; schema evolution has real limits
